Patient: Okay, doctor. What did the report say?
Doctor: It shows that you have a medical history of hypertension, type II diabetes mellitus, and ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy. Also, you have a history of heavy smoking for 30 years, am I correct?
Patient: Yes, that's correct.
Doctor: Unfortunately, your heart condition has worsened, and you have signs of systemic edema resulting in dyspnea, extreme fatigue, and hypotension.
Patient: Oh no, what does that mean?
Doctor: According to the Interagency Registry for Mechanically Assisted Circulatory Support (INTERMACS), you are categorized as having II effort capacity. You need serious inotropic support, and we need to place you in the 'bridge to transplant', status Ib category.
Patient: Okay, doctor. What's next?
Doctor: We will be implanting a centrifugal type flow LVAD (Heartmate III, St. Jude Medical, Abbott) and starting you on anticoagulation therapy with enoxaparin sodium 6000 IU subcutaneously twice daily.
Patient: Do I need to stay in the hospital for this?
Doctor: Yes, you will need to stay in the hospital for a few days after the operation. We need to monitor your condition and make sure that everything is going well.
Patient: Okay, doctor. I understand.
Doctor: Unfortunately, at post-operative day 20, you presented with melena accompanied by a fall in haemoglobin levels from 11 to 6.4 g/dL.
Patient: What does that mean?
Doctor: We did an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and found that you have gastric cancer located at the cardia starting 1.5 cm distal to the Z-line, protruding into the gastric lumen at the posterior wall.
Patient: Oh no, what can we do?
Doctor: Due to your high-risk cardiovascular condition, we maintained enoxaparin at the therapeutic level twice daily at 6000 IU. Biopsy indicated a signet-ring cell adenocarcinoma, but subsequent PET-CT demonstrated no distant organ metastasis.
Patient: Okay, what's the plan now?
Doctor: After necessary preoperative assessment by anaesthesiologists and cardiologists, and under full therapeutic anticoagulation protocol (enoxaparin sodium 6000 IU twice daily), it was decided to proceed with a proximal gastric resection due to potentially life-threatening upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage.
Patient: What does that mean for me?
Doctor: Since the LVAD was implanted at the left upper quadrant, we found that an upper midline incision was feasible, and proximal gastrectomy with extended D1 dissection was then performed. However, I'm sorry to report that you didn't survive the operation.

Doctor: Hi, I'm Dr. Hernandez. How are you feeling today?
Patient: Hi, doctor. I'm feeling fine. Just a little nervous.
Doctor: That's understandable. You were referred to me for an evaluation of an asymptomatic retinal hemorrhage detected in your right eye. Can you tell me about your medical history?
Patient: Sure. I don't have any major medical issues. My eyes have been healthy up until now.
Doctor: Okay, that's good to know. I see from your records that you have a history of complete posterior vitreous detachment in your right eye. Is that correct?
Patient: Yes, that's right.
Doctor: Your best-corrected visual acuity is 20/20 in each eye. That's great news. I'm going to perform an anterior segment examination and applanation tensions to check for any abnormalities. 
Patient: Okay.
Doctor: After the examination, I found that everything was unremarkable. However, during the ophthalmoscopic examination of your right eye, I identified subretinal hemorrhage surrounding a pigment epithelial detachment (PED) located above the superotemporal vascular arcade.
Patient: What does that mean?
Doctor: It means that there is bleeding and fluid accumulation in the area behind your retina. I also performed spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) and optical coherence tomography (OCT) B-scan with angiographic flow overlay to confirm the diagnosis. 
Patient: And what did those tests show?
Doctor: They demonstrated the presence of a PED accompanied by irregularities of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) profile. The OCT B-scan with angiographic flow overlay showed a peaked PED with intrinsic flow signal. 
Patient: I see.
Doctor: I also examined your left eye and found a PED nasal to the optic nerve characterized by a dome-shaped elevation of the RPE with a shallow irregular portion on SD-OCT. The angiographic flow overlay revealed intrinsic flow signal. 
Patient: What about the small drusen?
Doctor: Ah, yes. I did see multiple, small, cuticular drusen appearing as small hypoautofluorescent dots on fundus autofluorescence (FAF) in both eyes along the vascular arcades. 
Patient: What should we do now?
Doctor: Based on the results of the Indocyanine green angiography (ICGA), which showed focal areas of hyperfluorescence within the PEDs, indicative of AT1, and the OCT angiography en face slab, which demonstrated aneurysmal dilatation arising from a type 1 neovascular network, particularly evident in the right eye with active lesions, we need to initiate treatment with anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) therapy for your right eye. 
Patient: Okay, what does that involve?
Doctor: It's a type of injection that will be administered directly into the eye to help reduce the bleeding and fluid accumulation. You will need to come back for follow-up appointments to monitor your progress. 
Patient: Alright, I understand. 
Doctor: If you have any questions or concerns, don't hesitate to call our office. 
Patient: Thank you, doctor. 
Doctor: You're welcome. Take care. 
Patient's family: Excuse me, doctor. We're the patient's family. We're sorry to inform you that the patient has passed away due to complications related to the retinal hemorrhage.

Doctor: Hello, how can I help you today?
Patient: Hi, I reported to the oral and maxillofacial surgery department with a chief complaint of swelling over the left cheek.
Doctor: I see. How long have you had this swelling?
Patient: It's been there for three months now.
Doctor: Did you experience any trauma to the area before the swelling appeared?
Patient: No, I haven't had any previous history of trauma in the concerned area.
Doctor: Okay, let's take a look. On examination, I notice a gross facial asymmetry on the left side of your face due to the presence of a swelling. Was it causing any pain?
Patient: No, it was asymptomatic.
Doctor: The swelling is gradually progressing and extending from the infraorbital margin to the upper lip inferiorly, obliterating the nasolabial fold. There are no secondary changes noticed over the skin. Have you experienced any sensory deficit in relation to the facial structures?
Patient: No, I haven't noticed any problems with my facial structures.
Doctor: Good. On intraoral examination, I noticed a bicortical swelling on the left side extending from the labial frenum medially till the distal aspect of the deciduous second molar, obliterating the labial and buccal vestibule. Do you have any caries affecting your deciduous teeth?
Patient: Yes, I have mild caries affecting my deciduous teeth, but none involving the pulp.
Doctor: I see. We will need to do some imaging to get a better understanding of the situation. An orthopantomogram shows a well-defined unilocular radiolucent lesion circumscribing the permanent teeth buds of the central, lateral incisor, and canine in the second quadrant. It measures around 3 cm in its greatest dimension. 
Patient: Okay.
Doctor: We also found radiolucency extending superiorly till the infraorbital margin with the canine involved on the paranasal sinus view. The canine was in Nolla's stage 7 and the central and lateral incisors were in stage 8. 
Patient: I don't really understand.
Doctor: Based on the clinical and radiographic findings, we have made a provisional diagnosis of a dentigerous cyst. A differential diagnosis of unicystic ameloblastoma and a cyst involving the maxillary antrum were considered as well. Based on the above diagnosis, we will plan for decompression.
Patient: What does that mean?
Doctor: We will create a small opening in the cyst to relieve the pressure and allow it to slowly shrink. It's a simple procedure, and you should be able to go home the same day. 
Patient: Okay.
Doctor: If you have any more questions, feel free to ask. We will need to schedule a follow-up appointment to monitor the progress of the cyst.
Patient: Sure, thank you.
[Several months later, the patient's family is called in to discuss the patient's death due to complications from the cyst.]

Doctor: I understand. We performed an Arterial Doppler and found severe stenosis in your left superficial femoral artery and popliteal artery. We started you on cilostazol, but your symptoms didn't improve. We then did an Arteriography and found there was occlusion of the left popliteal artery.

Doctor: Hi, Mr. Smith. How are you feeling today?
Patient: Hmm, not so great, doctor. My left side of the scrotum and upper leg have been in pain for a while now.
Doctor: I see. Can you tell me more about the pain? When did it start?
Patient: It started about a week after I had a laparoscopic donor nephrectomy surgery for my sister.
Doctor: Okay, I see. And were you discharged from the hospital after the procedure?
Patient: Yes, I was discharged three days after the surgery.
Doctor: During the physical examination, were any abnormalities found?
Patient: No, but my scrotum was hypersensitive to touch (allodynia).

Patient: No, not really. I still couldn't work because of the pain.
Doctor: After three years of neuropathic pain, we suspected a nerve entrapment of the genitofemoral nerve (GFN) was the cause. We performed an exploratory laparoscopy and found a hemoclip used for closure of the ureter at the time of nephrectomy was in close relation to the GFN.
Patient: Oh wow, I had no idea.
Doctor: Yes, due to the local scarring, we couldn't assess the nerve damage. We cut the GFN proximally in a normal looking segment and confirmed through pathological analysis that nerve tissue was present. Within 2 weeks following surgery, you were completely pain-free and could return to your normal activities.
Patient: That's amazing, doctor. Thank you so much for your help.
Doctor: Of course, Mr. Smith. Please come in for a follow-up appointment in a few weeks to make sure everything is still okay.

Doctor: We recommend a radical cystourethrectomy procedure along with ileal conduit formation. Lymphadenectomy will not be performed in this case.

As these characteristics of the tumors were common to the two lesions, we considered that they were originally a continuous lesion before transurethral resection.
